meta.description: Charlotte Lucas says it in the 2005 film, not in “Pride and Prejudice”. In the novel she says something far colder.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are all fools in love'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Austen. A 2005 screen line — and the novel’s Charlotte is nothing like this warm.

answer.label: Not Jane Austen — a line from the 2005 film
answer.authorDates: born 28 June 1948 · English novelist and screenwriter
answer.sourceLine: Spoken by Charlotte Lucas in Joe Wright’s Pride & Prejudice (2005), where Deborah Moggach holds the sole screenplay credit ↗. The sentence is in none of Austen’s books. One caveat we will not hide: Wikipedia records ↗ that Emma Thompson worked on the script uncredited and made recommendations on “parts of the Collins–Charlotte storyline” — which is where this line sits — so the credit belongs to Moggach and the sentence itself may not.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: CHARLOTTE: We are all fools in love.
trail: Searched all eight Austen texts at Project Gutenberg, including Pride and Prejudice ↗, for “fools in love”. Zero matches.

Found the line in Wikiquote’s transcription of Pride and Prejudice (2005 film) ↗, attributed there to Charlotte. We have not viewed the film, so the attribution of the spoken line rests on that transcription, not on our own check of a print.

Read Charlotte’s actual position in chapter 6 of the novel ↗ — “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance” — which is the opposite sentiment, and is the reason her marriage to Mr Collins reads as a calculation rather than a folly.

Confirmed the credits against Wikipedia’s article on the film ↗: written by Deborah Moggach, directed by Joe Wright, UK release 16 September 2005. The same article notes Emma Thompson’s uncredited script work on the Collins–Charlotte material, which we report rather than resolve.
source.excerptNote: Set it against the Charlotte of the novel, chapter 6: “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance… it is better to know as little as possible of the defects of the person with whom you are to pass your life.” Austen’s Charlotte is a realist about marriage precisely because she does not believe anyone is a fool in love. The film softens her.

sourceLink.text: Pride and Prejudice (2005 film), transcribed dialogue at Wikiquote

source.rightsNote: In copyright — a 2005 screenplay is nowhere near public domain. We are deliberately not naming a rights holder: screen writing is work for hire, so the rights sit with the production rather than the writer, and we could not reach a source stating the film’s copyright line. Austen’s 1813 novel is public domain; this sentence is not part of it.

author.bio: Deborah Moggach (born 28 June 1948) is an English playwright, novelist and screenwriter, the author of nineteen novels including Tulip Fever (1999) and These Foolish Things (2004, filmed as The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel). She holds the sole screenplay credit on Joe Wright’s Pride & Prejudice (2005).

copyAttribution: Jane Austen did not write “We are all fools in love.” It is Charlotte Lucas’s line in the 2005 film of Pride & Prejudice, screenplay credited to Deborah Moggach. In the novel (ch. 6) Charlotte says the opposite: “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.” Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A screen line that has drifted onto Austen’s bookshelf — and onto the wrong Charlotte.

items.why: “fools in love” returns no match in the novel ↗ or anywhere else in Austen.
Wikiquote transcribes it ↗ as Charlotte’s line in the Joe Wright film.
She has the sole credit, but Wikipedia records ↗ Emma Thompson’s uncredited input on the Collins–Charlotte storyline. We name the credited writer and flag the doubt.
Chapter 6: “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.” The film makes her warmer than Austen wrote her.

misattribution.truthLine: Charlotte Lucas does say it — in 2005, on film. Austen’s Charlotte ↗ would have thought it sentimental.

context.heading: The most-rewritten character in Austen
lead: Charlotte Lucas is the novel’s cold shower. She marries a ridiculous man with her eyes open, explains her reasoning without apology, and is the strongest evidence that Pride and Prejudice is a book about money as much as feeling.

Adaptations tend to warm her up, because a modern audience finds her bargain hard to watch. “We are all fools in love” is that warming in a single sentence — and it is why the line reads as Austen-ish while saying something Austen’s Charlotte would not say.
